blocks.text: The conversion of Gallicanus, Commander-in-Chief. On the eve of his departure for a campaign against the Scythians, Gallicanus is betrothed to the Emperor Constantine’s daughter, Constance, a consecrated virgin.
When threatened with defeat in battle, Gallicanus is converted by John and Paul, Grand Almoners to Constance. He is immediately baptized and takes a vow of celibacy.

Later he is exiled by order of Julian the Apostate, and receives the crown of martyrdom. John and Paul are put to death by the same prince and buried secretly in their own house. Not long after, the son of their executioner becomes possessed by a devil. He is cured after confessing the crime committed by his father. He bears witness to the merits of the martyrs, and is baptized, together with his father.

Gallicanus, this tries my patience. You have delayed the offensive against the Scythians too long. The only nation which boldly resists our power and refuses to make peace with Rome! You know well enough that you were chosen because of your energy in your country’s service.
Most noble Constantine, I have served you hand and foot, ungrudgingly, devotedly, and have always striven to repay your trust in me with deeds. I have never shirked any task.
Is there any need to remind me? As if your great services were not always in mind! I spoke, not to reproach you, but to urge you to act quickly.
I will set out at once.
I am rejoiced to hear it.
I am ready to obey your orders if it costs me my life.
Your zeal pleases me. I appreciate your devotion.
As both are immense should they not be rewarded on the same scale?
It is easier for a man to undertake a difficult enterprise when he is sustained by the knowledge that his reward is sure.
I beg you then to promise me now my prize for this dangerous undertaking. In hard and strenuous fighting, when it seems as if I must be defeated, the thought of this reward will give me new strength.

The reward deemed by the Senate the most glorious a man can desire has never been withheld from you, and never shall be. You enjoy the freedom of my court, and the highest honour among those who surround me.
I know, but I am not thinking of that.
If you have other ambitions, you must tell me.
We shall see. I say you will be indignant.
Your fears are groundless. Come! Speak!
Since you command me, I will. I love Constance. I love your daughter.
That is well. You do right to love the daughter of your sovereign. Your love honours her.
You say this to cut me short.
I wish to marry her. Will you give your consent?
He asks no small thing, my lords. This is an honour of which none of you have ever dreamed.
Most illustrious Emperor, we beg you to be generous. Remember his services, and do not turn a deaf ear to his request.
I have not done so, but it is my duty first to make sure that my daughter consents.
I will go to her, and, if such is your wish, Gallicanus, I will lay the project before her.
Our Lord the Emperor approaches. He looks strangely grave and sad. What can it mean?
Constance, my child, come nearer. I wish to speak to you.
I am here, my lord. Command me.
I am in great distress of mind. My heart is heavy.
As you came in I saw that you were sad, and without knowing the reason I was troubled.
You frighten me. What is it, my lord?
The fear of grieving you ties my tongue.
You will grieve me more by keeping silence.
Gallicanus, my General, whose victories have won him the first place among the princes of my realm﻿—Gallicanus, whose sword is necessary for the defence of the Empire﻿—Gallicanus﻿—
He wants to make you his wife.
I knew that would be your answer.
It cannot surprise you, as it was with your consent and approval that I consecrated myself to God.
I will keep my vow inviolate. Nothing can ever force me to break it.

I know you are right, and the greater my difficulty. For if, as is my duty as your father, I permit you to be faithful to your vow, as a sovereign I shall suffer for it. Yet were I to oppose your resolution﻿—which God forbid!﻿—I should deserve eternal punishment.
If I despaired of divine help I should be more wretched than you.
But a heart which trusts in God’s goodness is armed against sorrow.
My lord, if you will deign to listen to my advice, I can show you how to escape this double danger.

You must pretend that you are willing to grant Gallicanus what he asks when the war has been won. Make him believe that I agree. Persuade him to leave with me during his absence at the war his two daughters, Attica and Anemia, as pledges of the bond of love which is to unite us. Tell him that in return I will send with him on his expedition my two Almoners, John and Paul.
And if he should return victorious? What then?
We must pray the Father of us all that he will change his mind.
My daughter, my daughter! Your sweet words have softened the harshness of your father’s grief! Henceforth I will not give way to anxiety.
I will return to Gallicanus and satisfy him with this promise.
O princes, I die of impatience to learn what has come of this long conference between our august sovereign and his daughter.
He promised to plead your cause.
Oh, that his arguments may prevail!
Peace! Silence all of you! The Emperor comes. His face is not anxious as when he left us, but serene and glad.
It is said that the face is the mirror of the soul. If this be true, the calm joy in his reflects a kindly mood.
Forward, forward. He is asking for you.
Now the good gods help me!
Gallicanus, set out for the war with an easy mind. On your return you shall receive the reward you covet.
I should be happy indeed if I could know one thing.
It is unreasonable to expect a young maid to answer in so many words. Events will prove that she consents.
If I could be assured of that, I should trouble little about the manner of her answer.
Then listen. She has given orders that her Almoners, John and Paul, shall stay with you until the day of your nuptials.
That by constant intercourse with them you may learn to know how she lives﻿—her habits and her tastes.
An excellent plan, and one that pleases me beyond measure.
She would like you in return to allow your two young daughters to live with her for the same period. She thinks she can learn from them how to please you.
Oh, joy, joy! All things are falling out as I wished.
Send for your daughters without delay.
Are my soldiers still there? Come, fellows, hasten! Run to my daughters and bring them to their sovereign’s presence.
Most noble Constance, the illustrious daughters of Gallicanus are here. They are beautiful, wise and virtuous, and in every way worthy of your friendship.
Hail, most noble Constance! Imperial highness, hail!
Greeting, my sisters, Artemia and Attica. Stand up, stand up! No, do not kneel. Salute me rather with a loving kiss.
We come joyfully to offer you our homage, lady. We are ready to serve you with our whole hearts, and we seek no reward but your love.

We have one Lord Who is in heaven. He alone should be served like that. We owe Him a love and fidelity which must be shown not only with whole hearts but with whole bodies. That is if we would enter His kingdom with the virgin’s palm.
We do not question this. You will find us eager to obey you in all things, but never so eager as when you exhort us to confess our faith and keep our vow of purity.
That is a good answer, and one worthy of a noble mind. I see that through divine grace you already have the faith.
How could we poor idolators have any good thought if light had not been given us from above?
The strength of your faith makes me hope that Gallicanus too will believe some day.
He has only to be taught. Then he must believe.
You sent for us, Highness. We are here.
Go at once to Gallicanus and attach yourselves to his person. Instruct him little by little in the mysteries of our faith. Perhaps God means to make us the instruments of winning him to His service.
God give us success! We shall do all we can.
You are welcome, John﻿—and you, Paul. I have awaited your coming with impatience.
As soon as we received our lady’s commands we hastened at once to put ourselves at your service.
Your offer to serve me gives me a pleasure that nothing else could give.
That is natural, for, as the saying goes, “The friends of our friends are our friends.”
The love our lady bears you assures us of your goodwill.
You can rely on it. Come, tribunes and centurions, assemble the troops. Soldiers in my command, I present to you John and Paul, for whose arrival our departure has been delayed.
We must first go to the Capitol, and visit the temples to propitiate the gods with the customary sacrifices. That is the way to obtain success for our arms.
Let us withdraw for a time.
The General is leaving the temple. Let us mount our horses and ride to meet him.
I noticed you were not with us. Where have you been?
We were seeing to our baggage. We have sent it on ahead that we may ride with you unencumbered.
By Jupiter, tribunes, I see the legions of an immense army advancing! The diversity of their arms is enough to make the stoutest heart tremble.
Let us resist with courage, and show them we are men!
It is useless to attempt resistance to such a host.
By Pollux, we must surrender! See, we are surrounded on every side﻿—we are being mown down﻿—we perish!
Ye gods! What will happen if the tribunes refuse to obey me, and surrender?
Promise you will become a Christian, and you will conquer.
I swear! And I will keep my vow.
Woe to us, King Bradan! Fortune, who but now promised us victory, was mocking us. Our men are weakening, their strength is exhausted﻿—they have lost heart and are giving up the struggle.
I am uncertain what to do. A strange faintheartedness has seized me also. There is but one course﻿—we must surrender.
There is nothing else to do.
Gallicanus, do not destroy us! Be merciful! Spare our lives and do with us what you will.
Have no fear. There is no need to tremble. Give me hostages, acknowledge yourselves tributaries of the Emperor, and you shall live happy under a Roman peace.
You have only to name the number and rank of the hostages, and the tribute to be exacted.
Soldiers, lay down arms. Slay no one, wound no one, but embrace as friends these men whom you had to fight as enemies of the Empire.
How much more powerful is one fervent prayer than all the pride of man!
What mighty succour God in His mercy sends to those who humbly trust in Him!
I have had good proof of it.
But the promise made when the storm was raging must be kept now it is calm.
I agree. It is my wish to be baptized as soon as possible, and to devote the rest of my life to the service of God.
Look! That vast crowd of citizens has gathered to see our entry into Rome! See how they flock to acclaim us, bearing according to custom the symbols of victory!
Yet the glorious victory was not won by my valour nor by the help of their gods.
No, assuredly; the glory belongs to the one true God.
That being so, we must pass the temples without going in.
And instead make a humble confession of faith in the Church of the Apostles.
O happy man! And most happy thought! In this you show yourself a true Christian.
I am greatly astonished, soldiers, that Gallicanus should be so long in presenting himself before his sovereign.
The moment he arrived in Rome he went to the Church of Saint Peter, and, prostrating himself on the ground, gave thanks to the Almighty for giving him the victory.
Here he comes. You can ask him yourself.
Welcome, Gallicanus! I have awaited your arrival with impatience. I long to hear from your own lips how the battle went and how it ended.
I will tell you the whole story.
Wait a moment, for even the battle is of small importance compared with the one thing which I want most to hear.
On your departure for the war you visited the temple of the gods; on your return you went to the Church of the Apostles. Why?
Have I not told you, man, that I wish to know above all things!
Most Sacred Emperor, I confess I visited the temples on my departure, as you have said, and humbly sought the help of gods and demons.
According to the old Roman custom.
To my thinking, a bad custom.
I am of the same mind.
Then the tribunes arrived with their legions and we began our march.
You set out from Rome with great pomp.
We pushed on, met the enemy, engaged them, and were defeated.
When was such a disaster ever known in our history!
Once again I offered those hideous sacrifices, but what god came to my help? The fury of the enemy redoubled, and great numbers of my men were slain.
It was then that the tribunes, disregarding my orders, began to surrender.
What could I do but take to flight?
What anguish for a man of your courage!
My faithful companions, John and Paul, advised me to make a vow to the Creator.
I found it so. Hardly had I opened my lips to make the vow than I received help from heaven.
A young man of immense stature appeared before me carrying a cross on his shoulder. He bade me follow him sword in hand.
This young man, whoever he was, was sent from heaven.
So it proved. At the same moment I saw at my side some soldiers whose faces were strange to me. They promised me their help.

I am sure of it. Following in the steps of my guide, I advanced fearlessly into the midst of the enemy until I came face to face with their King, by name Bradan. Suddenly overcome by the strangest terror he threw himself at my feet, surrendered with his whole army, and promised to pay tribute in perpetuity to the ruler of the Roman world.
Now praise be to Him Who gave us this victory. Those who put their trust in Him will never be confounded.
And now I should like to know what became of the treacherous tribunes?
They hastened to implore my forgiveness.
I show mercy to men who had abandoned me in the hour of peril and surrendered to the enemy against my orders! No, assuredly!
I offered to pardon them on one condition.

I told them that those who consented to become Christians would be allowed to retain their rank, and might even receive fresh honours, but that those who refused would not be pardoned, and would be degraded.
A fair proposition, and honourable to the leader who made it.

For my own part, purified in the waters of baptism, I have surrendered myself completely to the will of God. I am ready to renounce even your daughter, whom I love more than anything in the world. I wish to abstain from marriage that I may devote myself wholly to the service of the Virgin’s Son.
Come near, nearer yet, and let me fold you in my arms! Now, Gallicanus, the time has come for me to tell you what up to now I have been obliged to keep secret.
My daughter, and your own two also, have chosen the same holy path which you yourself wish to follow.
Their desire to keep their vow of virginity is so ardent that neither entreaties nor threats can alter their resolution.
Come, let us go to their apartments.
They are coming here. Look, they hasten to greet us, and my glorious mother, noble Helena, is with them. They all weep for joy.
Be at peace, most holy virgins. Persevere in the fear of God, and preserve untouched the treasure of your virginity. Then you will be worthy of the embraces of the eternal King.
We shall keep our vows with more joy now we know that you are on our side.

Have no fear that I shall put any obstacle in your way. Far from it! I consent gladly, and desire nothing better than to see you fulfil your vow, my Constance, you, for whom I was eager to risk life itself.
I see the hand of the Most High in this change in you.
If I had not changed, and for the better, I could never have consented to renounce you.

The Lover of virginal purity and the Author of all good resolutions made you renounce me because He had already claimed me for His own. May He Who has separated us in the body on earth unite us in the joys of eternity.
So be it! So be it!
And now, since we are united in the bond of Christ’s love, you shall live with us in our palace, and be treated with as much honour as though you were our own son.
What temptation is to be feared more than the lust of the eyes?
Then is it right that I should see her too often? As you know, I love her more than my own kin, more than my life, more than my soul!
You must do what you think best.

Thanks to our Lord Christ and to my labours, your army was never so strong as now. Give me leave, then, to transfer my service to that Emperor through Whose power I have returned victorious, and to Whom I owe any success I have won in life.
To Him be praise and glory. All creatures should serve Him.
Above all those whom He has generously helped in time of need.

I am giving to my daughters the portion of my property which is theirs by right. Another I am devoting to the support of pilgrims. With the remainder I propose to enrich my slaves﻿—whom I have freed﻿—and to relieve the poor.
You are disposing of your wealth wisely, and you will be rewarded.
As for me, I long to go to Ostia and become the disciple of the holy man, Hilarion. In his brotherhood I hope to spend the rest of my life praising God and helping the poor.

May the Divine Being to Whom all things are possible bring your plans to a happy issue! May you always do the will of Him Who lives and reigns in the Unity of the Trinity, and at last attain eternal joy!
The cause of the unrest in our Empire is clear enough. These Christians enjoy too much liberty. Their claim that they obey laws made in the time of Constantine is false.
It would be a disgrace to tolerate it.
I do not intend to tolerate it.
Those words are worthy of you.
Soldiers, arm yourselves and strip the Christians of all they possess. Remind them of these words of their Christ: “He who does not renounce all that he possesses for my sake cannot be my disciple.”
We will carry out your orders instantly.
Why have you returned so soon?

We will tell you. We had planned to seize Gallicanus’s castle and occupy it in your name. But no sooner did one of us set foot on the threshold than he was straightway stricken with leprosy or madness.
Return and force Gallicanus to quit the realm or sacrifice to the gods.

Do not waste your breath, fellows. Your advice is useless. I hold all that exists beneath the sun as nothing compared with eternal life. Banished for Christ’s sake, I shall retire to Alexandria, where I hope to win the martyr’s crown.
Gallicanus, exiled by your orders, fled to Alexandria. He was arrested in that city by the Governor, Ratianus, and has perished by the sword.
But John and Paul still defy you.
Travelling up and down the country giving away the fortune Constance left them.
John and Paul, from the cradle you have been attached to the Emperor’s household. You served my predecessor.
Then what could be more fitting than that you should serve me also in this palace where you were brought up?
Do you deny that I am Augustus?
No, but we say you are Augustus with a difference.
How do I differ from my predecessors?
In your religion and your virtue.
We mean that those most famous and glorious princes, Constantine, Constantius and Constance, whom we served, were very Christian rulers who were zealous in the service of God.
I know, but in this I do not choose to follow their example.
You follow worse examples. They frequented the churches and, laying their diadems on the ground, adored Jesus Christ on their knees.
And you think that I should imitate them?
You are not made of the same stuff.

By doing homage to the Creator they elevated the Imperial dignity﻿—yes, they transfigured it with the splendour of their virtue and their holy lives. So they deserved the success which crowned their enterprises.
In a very different way, for the divine grace was with them.
Absurd! Once I too was fool enough to believe in these meaningless practices. I was a priest of your Church.
Do you hear, Paul? How do you like this priest?
But when I found that there was nothing to be gained from it, I turned to the worship of the true Roman gods, thanks to whom I have been raised to the highest pinnacle of power.
You cut us short with this boast to avoid hearing the righteous praised.

Nothing; but we would add something which does concern you. When the world was no longer worthy of those princes, they were summoned to the choir of angels, and this unhappy realm fell under your power.
Because of the character of its ruler.
Have you not renounced the true religion and adopted the superstitions of idolatry? Because of this we have shunned you and your court.
You show yourselves greatly wanting in the respect due to me, yet I am ready to pardon your presumption and raise you to the highest office in my palace.
You waste your breath, apostate! We shall yield neither to blandishments nor threats.

I will give you ten days’ grace, in the hope that you will come to your senses and repent. If you do, you will regain our Imperial favour. If not, I shall do what I have to do. You shall not make a mock of me.
What you have to do, do now, for you can never make us return either to your court, your service, or your gods.
You are dismissed. Leave me, but heed my warning.
We willingly accept the respite you have granted us, but only that we may spend the time consecrating all our faculties to heaven, and commending ourselves to God in prayer and fasting.
This is all we have to do now.

Go, Terentianus. Take with you a few trusted soldiers and compel John and Paul to sacrifice to Jupiter. If they persist in their refusal, let them be put to death, not publicly, but with the greatest possible secrecy, since they once held office in this palace.
Paul and John, the Emperor Julian, my master, of his clemency sends you this gold statue of Jupiter, and commands you to burn incense before it. Refuse, and you will be put to death.

Since Julian is your master, live at peace with him, and enjoy his favour. But we have no master except our Lord Jesus Christ, for Whose love we ardently desire to die that we may the more quickly taste the joys of eternity.

Soldiers, why do you delay? Draw your swords and strike these traitors to the gods and to their Emperor. When they have breathed their last bury them secretly in this house and remove every trace of blood.
And if questions are asked, what are we to say?
To Thee, O Christ, Who reigneth with the Father and the Holy Ghost, one God, we raise our voices in this dreadful hour! In death as in life we praise Thee.
O Christ, receive our souls, which for Thy sake are being driven from this dwelling of clay!
Christians, Christians, what ails my son?
He grinds his teeth, foams at the mouth, and rolls his eyes like a madman. He is sure possessed by a devil.
Woe to his father! Where was he stricken?
Before the tomb of the martyrs John and Paul. He writhes on the ground, and cries out that they are the cause of his torments.
Mine the fault! Mine the crime! It was at my command that the wretched boy laid his impious hands on those holy martyrs.
Since you were the partner of his guilt, it is right that you should share his sufferings.
I did but obey the wicked commands of my master, the Emperor Julian.
He himself has been struck down by the divine wrath.
I know, and am the more terrified. I see that no enemy of those servants of God can escape punishment.
What if in expiation of my crime I threw myself on my knees before the holy tombs?
You would win pardon if you were first cleansed by baptism.

Glorious witnesses of Christ, John and Paul, follow the example and commandment of your Master, and pray for your persecutors. Have compassion on the anguish of a father who fears to lose his child! Have pity on the sufferings of the son! Succour us both, and grant that, purified in the waters of baptism, we may persevere in the faith.
Dry your tears, Terentianus. Here is balm for your anguish. Look! Your son has recovered his health and his reason through the intercession of the martyrs.

Praise to the Eternal King Who covers His servants with such glory! Not only do their souls rejoice in heaven, but in the depths of the sepulchre their lifeless bones work astounding miracles, testifying to their sanctity and to the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ Who liveth and reigneth!

The martyrdom of the holy virgins Agape, Chionia, and Irena. The Governor Dulcitius seeks them out in the silence of the night with criminal intent, but hardly has he entered their dwelling than he becomes the victim of a delusion, under which he mistakes for the objects of his passion the saucepans and frying-pans in the kitchen. These he embraces and covers with kisses until his face and clothes are black with soot and dirt. Later, by order of Diocletian, he hands the maidens over to the care of Sisinnius, who is charged with their punishment. Sisinnius in his turn is made the sport of the most strange delusions, but at length succeeds in getting Agape and Chionia burnt, and Irena shot to death with arrows.
Ladies-in-Waiting on the Wife of Dulcitius

The pure and famous race to which you belong and your own rare beauty make it fitting that you should be wedded to the highest in our court. Thus we decree, making the condition that you first promise to deny your Christ and sacrifice to the gods.
We beg you not to concern yourself about us, and it is useless to make preparations for our marriage. Nothing can make us deny that Name which all should confess, or let our purity be stained.
What sign of madness do you see in us?
In what way are we mad?
Is it not madness to give up practising an ancient religion and run after this silly new Christian superstition?
You are bold to slander the majesty of Almighty God. It is dangerous.
To you, and to the state you rule.
The girl raves. Take her away.
My sister does not rave. She is right.
This maenad seems even more violent than the other! Remove her also from our presence, and we will question the third.
You will find her as rebellious and as determined to resist.
Irena, you are the youngest in years. Show yourself the oldest in dignity.
Bow your head to the gods, and set an example to your sisters. It may rebuke and save them.

Let those who wish to provoke the wrath of the Most High prostrate themselves before idols! I will not dishonour this head which has been anointed with heavenly oil by abasing it at the feet of images.
The worship of the gods does not bring dishonour to those who practise it, but, on the contrary, the greatest honour.
What could be more shameful baseness, what baser shame, than to venerate slaves as if they were lords?
I do not ask you to worship slaves, but the gods of princes and the rulers of the earth.
A god who can be bought cheap in the marketplace, what is he but a slave?
Enough of this presumptuous chatter. The rack shall put an end to it!
That is what we desire. We ask nothing better than to suffer the most cruel tortures for the love of Christ.
Let these obstinate women who dare to defy our authority be laden with chains and thrown into a dungeon. Let them be examined by Governor Dulcitius.
The ones you wanted to see are in there.
Ye Gods, but these girls are beautiful! What grace, what charm!
I’m in love! Do you think they will fall in love with me?
From what we know, you will have little success.
A few sweet words will work wonders!
Then I shall woo in another fashion﻿—with torture!
That is for you to find out.
Lock them in the inner room﻿—the one leading out of the passage where the pots and pans are kept.
What can the prisoners be doing at this hour of night?
They pass the time singing hymns.
Now you can hear their silver-sweet voices in the distance.
Take your torches, and guard the doors. I will go in and enjoy myself in those lovely arms!
Enter. We will wait for you here.
What noise is that outside the door?
There is more noise! It sounds like the clashing of pots and pans and fire-irons.
I will go and look. Come quick and peep through the crack of the door!
Oh, look! He must be out of his senses! I believe he thinks that he is kissing us.
Now he presses the saucepans tenderly to his breast, now the kettles and frying-pans! He is kissing them hard!
His face, his hands, his clothes! They are all as black as soot. He looks like an Ethiope.
I am glad. His body should turn black﻿—to match his soul, which is possessed of a devil.
Look! He is going now. Let us watch the soldiers and see what they do when he goes out.
What’s this? Either one possessed by the devil, or the devil himself. Let’s be off!
Soldiers, soldiers! Why do you hurry away? Stay, wait! Light me to my house with your torches.
The voice is our master’s voice, but the face is a devil’s. Come, let’s take to our heels! This devil means us no good.
I will hasten to the palace. I will tell the whole court how I have been insulted.
Ushers, admit me at once. I have important business with the Emperor.
Who is this fearsome, horrid monster? Coming here in these filthy rags! Come, let us beat him and throw him down the steps. Stop him from coming further.

Ye gods, what has happened to me? Am I not dressed in my best? Am I not clean and fine in my person? And yet everyone who meets me expresses disgust at the sight of me and treats me as if I were some foul monster! I will go to my wife. She will tell me the truth. But here she comes. Her looks are wild, her hair unbound, and all her household follow her weeping.
My lord, my lord, what evil has come on you? Have you lost your reason, Dulcitius? Have the Christ-worshippers put a spell on you?
Now at last I know! Those artful women have made an ass of me!
What troubled me most, and made my heart ache, was that you should not know there was anything amiss with you.
Those impudent wenches shall be stripped and exposed naked in public. They shall have a taste of the outrage to which I have been subjected!

Here we are sweating like pigs and what’s the use? Their clothes cling to their bodies like their own skin. What’s more, our chief, who ordered us to strip them, sits there snoring, and there’s no way of waking him. We will go to the Emperor and tell him all that has passed.

I grieve to hear of the outrageous way in which the Governor Dulcitius has been insulted and hoaxed! But these girls shall not boast of having blasphemed our gods with impunity, or of having made a mock of those who worship them. I will entrust the execution of my vengeance to Count Sisinnius.
Soldiers, where are these impudent hussies who are to be put to the torture?
Keep Irena back, and bring the others here.
Why is one to be treated differently?
She is young, and besides she may be more easily influenced when not intimidated by her sisters.
We have brought the girls you asked for.
Agape, and you, Chionia, take my advice.
And if we do, what then?
You will sacrifice to the gods.
We offer a perpetual sacrifice of praise to the true God, the eternal Father, to His Son, co-eternal, and to the Holy Ghost.
I do not speak of that sacrifice. That is prohibited on pain of the most severe penalties.
You have no power over us, and can never compel us to sacrifice to demons.
Do not be obstinate. Sacrifice to the gods, or by order of the Emperor Diocletian I must put you to death.
Your Emperor has ordered you to put us to death, and you must obey, as we scorn his decree. If you were to spare us out of pity, you also would die.
Come, soldiers! Seize these blasphemers and fling them alive into the flames.
We will build a pyre at once. The fierceness of the fire will soon put an end to their insolence.

O Lord, we know Thy power! It would not be anything strange or new if the fire forgot its nature and obeyed Thee. But we are weary of this world, and we implore Thee to break the bonds that chain our souls, and to let our bodies be consumed that we may rejoice with Thee in heaven.
O wonderful, most wonderful! Their spirits have left their bodies, but there is no sign of any hurt. Neither their hair, nor their garments, much less their bodies, have been touched by the flames!
Irena, take warning from the fate of your sisters, and tremble, for if you follow their example you will perish.
I long to follow their example, and to die, that I may share their eternal joy.
I will yield to no man who persuades me to sin.
If you persist in your refusal, I shall not grant you a swift death. I shall eke it out and every day I shall increase and renew your torments.
The greater my pain, the greater my glory!
You are not afraid of being tortured, I know, but I can use another means that will be abhorrent to you.
By Christ’s help I shall escape from all you can devise against me.
I can send you to a house of ill-fame, where your body will be abominably defiled.
Better far that my body should suffer outrage than my soul.
When you are dishonoured and forced to live among harlots, you can no longer be numbered among the virgins.
The wage of sin is death; the wage of suffering a crown. If the soul does not consent, there is not guilt.
In vain I try to spare her, and show pity to her youth!
We could have told you as much. She is not to be frightened, and nothing can make her worship the gods.
I will show her no more mercy.
That is the only way to deal with her.
Have no pity. Be rough with her, and drag her to the lowest brothel you can find.
They will never take me there.
The power that rules the world.
Yes! Sooner than you will like!
Soldiers, do not let the absurd prophecies of this woman interfere with your duty.
We are not likely to be frightened by a slip of a girl! We will carry out your orders at once.

Who are these men hurrying towards us? They cannot be the soldiers who took away Irena. Yet they resemble them. Yes, these are the men! Why have you returned so suddenly? Why are you panting for breath?
We ran back to find you.
On the crest of the mountain.
The mountain yonder, nearest this place.
O fools, madmen! Have you lost your senses?
What’s the matter? Why do you look at us so threateningly, and speak with such anger?
May the gods crush you with their thunder!
What have we done? How have we offended? We have only obeyed your orders.
Fools! Did I not tell you to take this rebellious girl to a brothel?
That is so, but while we were on the way up came two young strangers and told us you had sent them to take Irena to the summit of the mountain.
I learn this for the first time from you.
They were gorgeously dressed and looked like people of rank.
They placed themselves one on each side of Irena, and told us to hasten and tell you what we had seen.
Then there is nothing to do but for me to mount my horse and ride to the mountain to discover who has dared to play us this trick.
What has happened to me? These Christians have bewitched me. I wander blindly round this hill, and when I stumble on a path I can neither follow it nor return upon my steps.
We are all the sport of some strange enchantment. We are exhausted. If you let this madwoman live an hour longer it will be the death of us all.
Take a bow one of you, bend it as far as you can, and loose a shaft that shall pierce this devilish witch.
You wretched Sisinnius! Do you not blush for your shameful defeat? Are you not ashamed that you could not overcome the resolution of a little child without resorting to force of arms?
I accept the shame gladly, since now I am sure of your death.

To me my death means joy, but to you calamity. For your cruelty you will be damned in Tartarus. But I shall receive the martyr’s palm, and, adorned with the crown of virginity, I shall enter the azure palace of the Eternal King, to Whom be glory and honour forever and ever!
The resurrection of Drusiana and Callimachus.

Callimachus cherishes a guilty passion for Drusiana, not only while she is alive but after she has died in the Lord. He dies from the bite of a serpent, but, thanks to the prayers of Saint John the Apostle, he is restored to life, together with Drusiana, and is born again in Christ.
My friends, a word with you.
We are at your service as long as you please.
I should prefer to speak with you apart from the crowd.
Then we will go to some quieter place where no one will interrupt us.
For a long time now I have been in great trouble. I hope that by confiding in you I shall find relief.
When a man tells his friends of his sufferings it is only fair that they should try to share them.
I would to heaven that you could lighten this load upon my heart!
Well, tell us precisely what is wrong. We will grieve with you, if we must. If not, we can do our best to distract your mind.
A thing of beauty, a thing of grace!
That is too vague! How can we tell from this what is the object of your love?
Ah, now you say “woman” we all understand!
By woman, I mean a woman.
Clearer still! But it is impossible to give an opinion on a subject until the subject is defined. So name the woman.
What? The wife of Prince Andronicus?
Nothing can come of that. She has been baptized.
What do I care, if I can win her love?
You are crying for the moon.
Am I the first to do so? Have I not the example of many others to encourage me?

Now listen. This woman you sigh for is a follower of the holy Apostle John, and has devoted herself entirely to God. They say she will not even go to the bed of Andronicus although he is a devout Christian. Is it likely that she will listen to you?
I came to you for consolation, and instead you drive me to despair!
We should be poor friends if we consoled and flattered you at the expense of the truth.
Since you refuse to advise me, I will go to her and pour out my soul in words that would melt a heart of stone!
Drusiana, listen to me! Drusiana, my deepest heart’s love!
Your words amaze me, Callimachus. What can you want of me?
First I want to speak of love!
That love with which I love you above all created things.
Why should you love me? You are not of my kin. There is no legal bond between us.
What is my beauty to you?
But little now﻿—it is that which tortures me﻿—but I hope that it may be much before long.
Not a word more. Leave me at once, for it is a sin to listen to you now that I understand your devilish meaning.
My Drusiana, do not kill me with your looks. Do not drive away one who worships you, but give back love for love.
Wicked, insidious words! They fall on deaf ears. Your love disgusts me. Understand I despise you!
You cannot make me angry, because I know that you would own my passion moves you if you were not ashamed.
It moves me to indignation, nothing else.
I shall not change, be sure of that.
I would not be too sure.
You frantic, foolish man! Do not deceive yourself! Why delude yourself with vain hopes? What madness leads you to think that I shall yield? I have renounced even what is lawful﻿—my husband’s bed!
I call heaven and earth to witness that if you do not yield I will never rest from the fight for you. I will be as cunning as the serpent. I will use all my skill and strength to trap you.

O Lord Jesus, what use is my vow of chastity? My beauty has all the same made this man love me. Pity my fears, O Lord. Pity the grief which has seized me. I know not what to do. If I tell anyone what has happened, there will be disorder in the city on my account; if I keep silence, only Thy grace can protect me from falling into the net spread for me. O Christ, take me to Thyself. Let me die swiftly. Save me from being the ruin of a soul!
Drusiana, Drusiana! Christ, what blow has fallen on me! Drusiana is dead. Run one of you and fetch the holy man John.
Why do you weep, my son?
Oh, horrible! O Lord, that life should suddenly become so hateful!
She has passed from the sight of men?
It is not right to mourn so bitterly for those whose souls we know rejoice in peace.

God knows I do not doubt that her soul is in eternal joy, and that her incorrupt body will rise again. What grieves me so sorely is that in my presence just now she prayed for death. She begged she might die.
I know it, and will tell you when I am less sick with grief.
Come. We must celebrate the funeral rites with proper ceremony.
There is a marble tomb near here in which the body shall be laid, and our steward Fortunatus shall guard her grave.
It is right that she should be interred with honour. God rest her soul in peace.
Fortunatus, Fortunatus, what is to become of me? Death itself cannot quench my love for Drusiana!
I shall die if you do not help me.
In this. You can let me look on her, dead.
Up to now the body is sound and whole, I reckon because it was not wasted with disease. As you know she was taken in a moment by a fever.
Oh, how happy I should be if I might see for myself.
If you are willing to pay me well, you can do what you like.
Here, take all I have with me, and be sure that I will give you more, much more, later.
Quick, then! We’ll go to the tomb.
You cannot go quickly enough for me.
There lies the body. The face is not like the face of a corpse. The limbs show no sign of decay. You can take her to your heart.

O Drusiana, Drusiana, I worshipped you with my whole soul! I yearned from my very bowels to embrace you! And you repulsed me, and thwarted my desire. Now you are in my power, now I can wound you with my kisses, and pour out my love on you.
Take care! A monstrous serpent! It is coming towards us!
A curse on me! And on you, Fortunatus, who led me on and urged me to this infamy. Wretch, may you die from the serpent’s bite! Terror and remorse are killing me.
Come, Andronicus, let us go to Drusiana’s tomb, and commend her soul to Christ in prayer.
It is like your holiness not to forget one who trusted in you.
Behold! The invisible God appears to us, made visible in the form of a beautiful youth.
Lord Jesus, why hast Thou deigned to manifest Thyself to Thy servants in this place?
To raise Drusiana from the dead, and with her him who lies outside her tomb, have I come, that in them My Name may be glorified.
How swiftly He was caught up again into heaven!
I cannot altogether understand what this means.
Let us go on to the tomb. It may be that there what is now obscure will become clear.
In Christ’s name, what miracle is this? The sepulchre is open, and Drusiana’s body has been cast forth. And near it lie two other corpses enlaced in a serpent’s coils.

I begin to understand. This is Callimachus, who while he lived was consumed with an unholy passion for Drusiana. It troubled her greatly and her distress brought on a fever. She prayed that she might die.
Such was her love of chastity.
After her death the wretched man, crazed with love, and stung by the defeat of his wicked plan, was still more inflamed by desire.
I have no doubt that he bribed this unworthy servant to give him the opportunity for committing a detestable crime.
It is not to be believed!
But death struck both of them down before the deed was accomplished.

What astonishes me most is that the Divine Voice should have promised the resurrection of him who planned the crime, and not of him who was only an accomplice. Maybe it is because the one, blinded by the passion of the flesh, knew not what he did, while the other sinned of deliberate malice.

With what wonderful exactness the Supreme Judge examines the deeds of men! How even the scales in which He weighs the merits of each individual man! None can understand, none explain. Human wisdom cannot grasp the subtlety of the divine judgment.
So we should be content to marvel at it, as it is not in our power to attain a precise knowledge of the causes of things.
Often the sequel teaches us to understand better.
Then, blessed John, do now what you were told to do. Raise Callimachus to life, and the knot of our perplexity may be untied.
First I must invoke the name of Christ to drive away the serpent. Then Callimachus shall be raised.
You are right; else the venom of the creature might do him fresh injury.
Hence, savage monster! Away from this man, for now he is to serve Christ.
Although the beast has no reason, it heeds your command.
Not through my power, but through Christ’s, it obeys me.
Look! As swift as thought it has vanished!

O God, the world cannot contain nor the mind of man comprehend the wonders of Thy incalculable unity, Thou Who alone art what Thou art! O Thou Who by mingling different elements canst create man, and by separating those elements again canst dissolve him, grant that the spirit and the body of this Callimachus may be joined once more, and that he may rise again wholly as he was, so that all looking on him may praise Thee, Who alone canst work miracles!
Look! The breath of life stirs in him again, but he does not move.
Calhmachus! In the name of Christ, arise, and confess your sin! Do not keep back the smallest grain of the truth.
I cannot deny that I came here for an evil purpose, but the pangs of love consumed me. I was beside myself.
What mad folly possessed you? That you should dare think of such a shameful outrage to the chaste dead!
Yes, I was mad; but this knave Fortunatus led me on.
And now, most miserable man, confess! Were you so vile as to do what you desired?
No! I could think of it, but I could not do it.
I had hardly touched the lifeless body﻿—I had hardly drawn aside the shroud, when that fellow there, who has been the spark to my fire, died from the serpent’s poison.

At the same moment there appeared to me a young man, beautiful yet terrible, who reverently covered the corpse again. From his flaming face and breast burning coals flew out, and one of them, falling on me, touched my face. I heard a voice say, “Callimachus, die to live!” It was then I breathed my last.
Oh, heavenly grace! God delights not in the damnation of the wicked.
You have heard the dreadful tale of my temptation. I beg you not to delay the merciful remedy.
I am overwhelmed by the thought of my abominable crime. I repent with my whole heart, and bewail my sin.
That is but right, for a great fault must be atoned for by a great repentance.
Oh, if I could lay bare my heart and show you the bitter anguish I suffer, you would pity me!
Not so. Rather does your suffering fill me with joy, for I know that it will be your salvation.
I loathe the delights of the flesh, and all the sins of my past life.
I truly repent my foul deed.
I am filled with such remorse that I have no desire to live unless I can be born again in Christ and changed.
I do not doubt that heavenly grace is at work in you.

Oh, hasten then to help a man in dire need! Give me some comfort! Help me to throw off the grief which crushes me! Show me how a Pagan may change into a Christian, a fornicator into a chaste man! Oh, set my feet on the way of truth! Teach me to live mindful of the divine promises!

Now blessed be the only Son of God, Who made Himself partaker of our frailty, and showed you mercy, my son Callimachus, by striking you down with the death which has brought you to the true life. So has He saved the creature He made in His own image from the death of the soul.

O Christ, redemption of the world, and sinners’ atonement, I have no words to praise Thee! The sweetness of Thy compassion amazes me. Now Thou dost win the sinner with gentleness, now Thou dost chastise him with just severity, and callest on him to do penance.

Who would have presumed to hope that a man like this, intent on a wicked deed when death overtook him, would be raised to life again, and given the chance of making reparation! Blessed be Thy name forever and ever, O Thou Who alone canst do these wondrous things!
Holy John, give me some comfort too. The love I bear my dead wife will not let me rest until I have seen her also called back from the dead.
Drusiana, our Lord Jesus Christ calls you back to life!
Glory and praise to Thee, O Lord, Who hast made me live again!
Thanks be to that merciful power, my Drusiana, through which you, who left this life in such sorrow, rise again in joy!
Venerable father John, you have restored to life Callimachus, who loved me sinfully. Should you not also raise from the dead the man who betrayed my buried body?
Apostle of Christ, do not believe it! Will you release from the fetters of death this evil creature, this traitor, who led me away and persuaded me to venture on that horrible deed?
You should not wish to deprive him of divine mercy, my son.
He tried to ruin me! He is not worthy of resurrection!
We are taught by our faith that man must forgive his fellow-man if he would be forgiven by God.
Remember that when the only Son of God, the Virgin’s firstborn, the one man born without a stain, came into this world, He found us all bowed under the heavy weight of sin.
And though not one of us was guiltless, He deprived no one of His mercy, but offered Himself for all, and for all laid down His life in love.
Had the Innocent One not been slain, none of us would have been saved.
He cannot rejoice in the damnation of those whom He bought with His blood.
This is why we must not grudge the grace of God to anyone. It is no merit of ours if it abounds in ourselves.
Yet it is not for me to oppose you. Drusiana, inspired by God Himself shall raise this man.

Divine Essence without material form, Who hast made man in Thine own image and breathed into this clay the spirit of life, bring back the vital heat to the body of Fortunatus, that our triple resurrection may glorify the adorable Trinity.
Fortunatus, awake, and in the name of Christ burst the bonds of death.
Who wakes me? Who takes my hand? Who calls me back to life?
How can that be? Only a few days since she died.
Yes, but now, through the power of Christ, she lives again.
And is that Callimachus who stands there? By his sober and pious look one would think he is no longer dying of love for his Drusiana!
All that is changed. Now he loves and serves Christ.
If it is as you say, if Drusiana has restored me to life and Callimachus believes in Christ, I reject life and choose death. I would rather not exist than see them swelling with grace and virtue!

Oh, incredible envy of the devil! Oh, malice of the old serpent, who since he made our first parents taste death has never ceased to writhe at the glory of the righteous! Oh, Fortunatus, brimful of Satan’s bitter gall, how much do you resemble the rotten tree that, bearing only bad fruit, must be cut down and cast into the fire! To the fire you must go, where, deprived of the society of those who fear God, you will be tormented without respite forever.
Look! Oh, look! His wounds have opened again. He has been taken at his word. He is dying.
Let him die and go down to hell, who through envious spite rejected the gift of life.
Nothing is more terrible than envy, nothing more evil than pride.
The man who is the victim of one is the victim of the other, for they have no separate existence.

The proud are envious, and the envious are proud. A jealous man cannot endure to hear others praised, and seeks to belittle those who are more perfect. He disdains to take a lower place, and arrogantly seeks to be put above his equals.
This wretched man’s pride was wounded. He could not endure the humiliation of recognizing his inferiority to these two in whom he could not deny God had made more grace to shine.
I understand now why his resurrection was not spoken of. It was known he would die again.
He deserved to die twice, for to his crime of profaning the sacred grave entrusted to him, he added hatred and envy of those who had been restored to life.
The wretched creature is dead now.

Come, let us go﻿—Satan must have his own. This day shall be kept as a festival in thanksgiving for the wonderful conversion of Callimachus. Men shall long speak of it, and of his resurrection from the dead, and of Drusiana, on whom his love brought misery. Let us give thanks to God, that just and penetrating Judge Who alone can search the heart and reins and reward or punish fairly. To Him alone be honour, strength, glory, praise, and blessing, world without end. Amen.

The fall and repentance of Mary, the niece of the hermit Abraham, who, after she has spent twenty years in the religious life as a solitary, abandons it in despair, and, returning to the world, does not shrink from becoming a harlot. But two years later Abraham, in the disguise of a lover, seeks her out and reclaims her. For twenty years she does penance for her sins with many tears, fastings, vigils, and prayers.
Brother Ephrem, my dear comrade in the hermit life, may I speak to you now, or shall I wait until you have finished your divine praises?
And what can you have to say to me which is not praise of Him Who said: “Where two or three are gathered together in My Name, I am with them”?
I have not come to speak of anything which He would not like to hear.
I am sure of it. So speak at once.
It concerns a decision I have to make. I long for your approval.
We have one heart and one soul. We ought to agree.
I have a little niece of tender years. She has lost both her parents, and my affection for her has been deepened by compassion for her lonely state. I am in constant anxiety on her account.
Ought you who have triumphed over the world to be vexed by its cares!
My only care is her radiant beauty! What if it should one day be dimmed by sin.
No one can blame you for being anxious.
At the end of this year she will be eight.
That does not lessen my anxiety.
At my hermitage now; for at the request of her other kinsfolk I have undertaken to bring her up. The fortune left her ought, I think, to be given to the poor.
A mind taught so early to despise temporal things should be fixed on heaven.
I desire with all my heart to see her the spouse of Christ and devoted entirely to His service.
I was inspired by her name.
Mary! Such a name ought to be adorned with the crown of virginity.
I have no fear that she will be unwilling, but we must be gentle.
Come, let us go, and impress on her that no life is so sweet and secure as the religious one.

Mary, my child by adoption, whom I love as my own soul! Listen to my advice as to a father’s, and to Brother Ephrem’s as that of a very wise man. Strive to imitate the chastity of the holy Virgin whose name you bear.
Child, would it not be a shame if you, who through the mystery of your name are called to mount to the stars where Mary the mother of God reigns, chose instead the low pleasures of the earth?
I know nothing about the mystery of my name, so how can I tell what you mean?
Mary, my child, means “star of the sea”﻿—that star which rules the world and all the peoples in the world.
Why is it called the star of the sea?
Because it never sets, but shines always in the heavens to show mariners their right course.
And how can such a poor thing as I am﻿—made out of slime, as my uncle says﻿—shine like my name?
By keeping your body unspotted, and your mind pure and holy.
It would be too great an honour for any human being to become like the stars.

If you choose you can be as the angels of God, and when at last you cast off the burden of this mortal body they will be near you. With them you will pass through the air, and walk on the sky. With them you will sweep round the zodiac, and never slacken your steps until the Virgin’s Son takes you in His arms in His mother’s dazzling bridal room!
Who but an ass would think little of such happiness! So I choose to despise the things of earth, and deny myself now that I may enjoy it!
Out of the mouths of babes and sucklings! A childish heart, but a mature mind!
But though by God’s grace she has been given the light, at her tender age she must be taught how to use it.
I will build her a little cell with a narrow entrance near my hermitage. I can visit her there often, and through the window instruct her in the psalter and other pages of the divine law.
I put myself under your direction, Father Ephrem.
My daughter! May the Heavenly Bridegroom to Whom you have given yourself in the tender bud of your youth shield you from the wiles of the devil!
Brother Ephrem, Brother Ephrem! When anything happens, good or bad, it is to you I turn. It is your counsel I seek. Do not turn your face away, brother﻿—do not be impatient, but help me.
Abraham, Abraham, what has come to you? What is the cause of this immoderate grief? Ought a hermit to weep and groan after the manner of the world?
Was any hermit ever so stricken? I cannot bear my sorrow.
Brother, no more of this. To the point; what has happened?
Mary! Mary! my adopted child! Mary, whom I cared for so lovingly and taught with all my skill for ten years! Mary﻿—
Most miserably. Afterwards she ran away.
But by what wiles did the ancient enemy bring about her undoing?

By the wiles of false love. Dressed in a monk’s habit, the hypocrite went to see her often. He succeeded in making the poor ignorant child love him. She leapt from the window of her cell for an evil deed.
I shudder as I listen to you.
When the unhappy girl knew that she was ruined, she beat her breast and dug her nails into her face. She tore her garments, pulled out her hair. Her despairing cries were terrible to hear.
I am not surprised. For such a fall a whole fountain of tears should rise.
She moaned out that she could never be the same﻿—
And reproached herself for having forgotten our warning.
She cried that all her vigils, prayers, and fasts had been thrown away.
If she perseveres in this penitence she will be saved.
She has not persevered. She has added worse to her evil deed.
Oh, this moves me to the depths of my heart!
After all these tears and lamentations she was overcome by remorse, and fell headlong into the abyss of despair.
She despaired of being able to win pardon, and resolved to go back to the world and its vanities.
I cannot remember when the devil could boast of such a triumph over the hermits.
Now we are at the mercy of the demons.
I marvel that she could have escaped without your knowledge.
If I had not been so blind! I ought to have paid more heed to that terrible vision. Yes, I see now that it was sent to warn me.

I dreamed I was standing at the door of my cell, and that a huge dragon with a loathsome stench rushed violently towards me. I saw that the creature was attracted by a little white dove at my side. It pounced on the dove, devoured it, and vanished.
There is no doubt what this vision meant.

When I woke I turned over in my mind what I had seen, and took it as a sign of some persecution threatening the Church, through which many of the faithful would be drawn into error. I prostrated myself in prayer, and implored Him Who knows the future to enlighten me.
On the third night after the vision, when for weariness I had fallen asleep, I saw the beast again, but now it was lying dead at my feet, and the dove was flying heavenwards safe and unhurt.
I am rejoiced to hear this, for to my thinking it means that some day Mary will return to you.

I was trying to get rid of the uneasiness with which the first vision had filled me by thinking of the second, when my little pupil in her cell came to my mind. I remembered, although at the time I was not alarmed, that for two days I had not heard her chanting the divine praises.
You were too tardy in noticing this.
I admit it. I went at once to her cell, and, knocking at the window, I called her again and again, “Mary! My child! Mary!”
“Mary,” I said. “Mary, my child, what is wrong? Why are you not saying your office?” It was only when I did not hear the faintest sound that I suspected.
When I could no longer doubt that she had gone, I was struck with fear to my very bowels. I trembled in every limb.
I do not wonder, since I, hearing of it, find myself trembling all over.
Then I wept and cried out to the empty air, “What wolf has seized my lamb? What thief has stolen my little daughter?”
You had good cause to weep! To lose her whom you had cherished so tenderly!
At last some people came up who knew what had happened. From them I learned that she had gone back to the world.
I have a faithful friend, who is searching all the cities and towns in the country. He says he will never give up until he finds her.
And if he finds her﻿—what then?

Then I shall change these clothes, and in the guise of a worldling seek her out. It may be that she will heed what I say, and even after this shipwreck turn again to the harbour of her innocence and peace.
And suppose that in the world they offer you flesh meat and wine?
If they do, I shall not refuse; otherwise I might be recognized.
No one will blame you, brother. It will be but praiseworthy discretion on your part to loosen the bridle of strict observance for the sake of bringing back a soul.
I am the more eager to try now I know you approve.

He Who knows the secret places of the heart can tell with what motive every action is done. That scrupulous and fair Judge will not condemn a man for relaxing our strict rule for a time and descending to the level of weaker mortals if by so doing he can make more sure of rescuing an errant soul.
Help me with your prayers. Pray that I may not be caught in the snares of the devil.
May He Who is supreme good itself, without Whom no good thing can be done, bless your enterprise and bring it to a happy end!
Can that be my friend who two years ago went to search for Mary? Yes, it is he!
Good day, dear friend. I have waited so long for you. Of late I had begun to despair.
Forgive me, father. I delayed my return because I did not wish to mock you with doubtful and unreliable news. As soon as I had discovered the truth I lost no time.
Where is she? Come, sir, speak! Tell me where.
It goes to my heart to tell you.
She lives in the house of a man who trades in the love of young girls like her. A profitable business, for every day he makes a large sum of money out of her lovers.
Good Jesu, what is this monstrous thing I hear? Do they say that she, whom I brought up to be Thy bride, gives herself to strange lovers?
If you are my friend, get me a saddle-horse somewhere and a soldier’s dress. I am going to get into that place as a lover.
Father, mine are at your service.
And I must borrow a felt hat to cover my tonsure.
That is most necessary, if you do not want to be recognized.
I have one gold piece. Should I take it to give this man?
You should, for otherwise he will never let you see Mary.
Who’s there? Good day, Sir. Come in!
Have you a bed for a traveller who wants to spend a night here?
Why certainly! I never turn anyone away.
Come in then, and I will order supper for you.
I owe you thanks for this kind welcome, but I have a greater favour to ask.
Ask what you like. I will do my best for you.
Accept this small present. May the beautiful girl who, I am told, lives here, have supper with me?
Why should you wish to see her?
It would give me much pleasure. I have heard so much talk of her beauty.
Whoever has spoken to you of her has told only the truth. It would be hard to find a finer wench.
I am in love with her already.
It’s queer that an old man like you should dangle after a young girl.
I swear I came here on purpose to feast my eyes on her.
Mary, come here! Come along now and show off your charms to this young innocent!

Oh, mind, be constant! Tears, do not fall! Must I look on her whom I brought up in the desert, decked out with a harlot’s face? Yes, I must hide what is in my heart. I must strive not to weep, and smile though my heart is breaking.
Luck comes your way, Mary! Not only do young gallants of your own age flock to your arms, but even the wise and venerable!
It is all one to me. It is my business to love those who love me.
Come nearer, Mary, and give me a kiss.
I will give you more than a kiss. I will take your head in my arms and stroke your neck.
What does this mean? What is this lovely fragrance. So clean, so sweet. It reminds me of the time when I was good.
On with the mask! Chatter, make lewd jests like an idle boy! She must not recognize me, or for very shame she may fly from me.
Wretch that I am! To what have I fallen! In what pit am I sunk!
You forget where you are! Do men come here to see you cry!
What’s the matter, Lady Mary? Why are you in the dumps? You have lived here two years, and never before have I seen a tear, never heard a sigh or a word of complaint.
Oh, that I had died three years ago before I came to this!
I came here to make love to you, not to weep with you over your sins.
A little thing moved me, and I spoke foolishly. It is nothing. Come, let us eat and drink and be merry, for, as you say, this is not the place to think of one’s sins.
I have eaten and drunk enough, thanks to your good table, Sir. Now by your leave I will go to bed. My tired limbs need a rest.
Get up my lord. I will take you to bed.
I hope so. I would not go at all unless you came with me.
Look! How do you like this room? A handsome bed, isn’t it? Those trappings cost a lot of money. Sit down and I will take off your shoes. You seem tired.
First bolt the door. Someone may come in.
Have no fear. I have seen to that.

The time has come for me to show my shaven head, and make myself known! Oh, my daughter! Oh, Mary, you who are part of my soul! Look at me. Do you not know me? Do you not know the old man who cherished you with a father’s love, and wedded you to the Son of the King of Heaven?
God, what shall I do! It is my father and master Abraham!
What has come to you, daughter?
Who deceived you? Who led you astray?
Have you forgotten that once you lived like an angel on earth!
What has become of your virginal modesty? Your beautiful purity?

Oh, Mary, think what you have thrown away! Think what a reward you had earned by your fasting, and prayers, and vigils. What can they avail you now! You have hurled yourself from heavenly heights into the depths of hell!
Could you not trust me? Why did you desert me? Why did you not tell me of your fall? Then dear brother Ephrem and I could have done a worthy penance.
Once I had committed that sin, and was defiled, how could I dare come near you who are so holy?
Oh, Mary, has anyone ever lived on earth without sin except the Virgin’s Son?
It is human to sin, but it is devilish to remain in sin. Who can be justly condemned? Not those who fall suddenly, but those who refuse to rise quickly.
Wretched, miserable creature that I am!
Why have you thrown yourself down there? Why do you lie on the ground without moving or speaking? Get up, Mary! Get up, my child, and listen to me!
No! no! I am afraid. I cannot bear your reproaches.
Remember how I love you, and you will not be afraid.

What but love for you could have made me leave the desert and relax the strict observance of our rule? What but love could have made me, a true hermit, come into the city and mix with the lascivious crowd? It is for your sake that these lips have learned to utter light, foolish words, so that I might not be known! Oh, Mary, why do you turn away your face from me and gaze upon the ground? Why do you scorn to answer and tell me what is in your mind.
It is the thought of my sins which crushes me. I dare not look at you; I am not fit to speak to you.
My little one, have no fear. Oh, do not despair! Rise from this abyss of desperation and grapple God to your soul!
No, no! My sins are too great. They weigh me down.

The mercy of heaven is greater than you or your sins. Let your sadness be dispersed by its glorious beams. Oh, Mary, do not let apathy prevent your seizing the moment for repentance. It matters not how wickedness has flourished. Divine grace can flourish still more abundantly!
If there were the smallest hope of forgiveness, surely I should not shrink from doing penance.

Have you no pity for me? I have sought you out with so much pain and weariness! Oh shake off this despair which we are taught is the most terrible of all sins. Despair of God’s mercy﻿—for that alone there is no forgiveness. Sin can no more embitter His sweet mercy than a spark from a flint can set the ocean on fire.
I know that God’s mercy is great, but when I think how greatly I have sinned, I cannot believe any penance can make amends.
I will take your sins on me. Only come back and take up your life again as if you had never left it.
I do not want to oppose you. What you tell me to do I will do with all my heart.
My daughter lives again! I have found my lost lamb and she is dearer to me than ever.
I have a few possessions here﻿—a little gold and some clothes. What ought I to do with them?
What came to you through sin, with sin must be left behind.
Could it not be given to the poor, or sold for an offering at the holy altar?
The price of sin is not an acceptable offering to God.
Then I will not trouble any more about my possessions.
Look! The dawn! It is growing light. Let us go.
You go first, dearest father, like the good shepherd leading the lost lamb that has been found. The lamb will follow in your steps.
Not so! I am going on foot, but you﻿—you shall have a horse so that the stony road shall not hurt your delicate feet.

Oh, let me never forget this tenderness! Let me try all my life to thank you! I was not worth pity, yet you have shown me no harshness; you have led me to repent not by threats but by gentleness and love.
I ask only one thing, Mary. Be faithful to God for the rest of your life.
With all my strength I will persevere, and though my flesh may fail, my spirit never will.
You must serve God with as much energy as you have served the world.
If His will is made perfect in me it will be because of your merits.
Come, let us hasten on our way.
Yes, let us set out at once. I would not stay here another moment.
Courage, Mary! You see how swiftly we have made the difficult and toilsome journey.
Everything is easy when we put our hearts into it.
There is your deserted little cell.
God help me! It was the witness of my sin. I dare not go there.
It is natural you should dread the place where the enemy triumphed.
Where, then, am I to do penance?
Go into the inner cell. There you will be safe from the wiles of the serpent.
Most gladly as it is your wish.
Now I must go to my good friend Ephrem. He alone mourned with me when you were lost, and he must rejoice with me now that you have been found.
Well, brother! If I am not mistaken, you bring good news.
You have found your lost lamb?
I have, and, rejoicing, have brought her back to the fold.
Truly this is the work of divine grace.
How is she spending her days? I should like to know how you have ordered her life. What does she do?
Nothing is too difficult for her﻿—nothing too hard. She is ready to endure anything.
She wears a hair shirt, and subdues her flesh with continual vigils and fasts. She is making the poor frail body obey the spirit by the most rigorous discipline.
Only through such a severe penance can the stains left by the pleasures of the flesh be washed away.
Those who hear her sobs are cut to the heart, and the tale of her repentance has turned many from their sins.
She prays continually for the men who through her were tempted to sin, and begs that she who was their ruin may be their salvation.
It is right that she should do this.
She strives to make her life as beautiful as for a time it was hideous.
I rejoice at what you tell me. To the depths of my heart.
And with us rejoice phalanxes of angels, praising the Lord for the conversion of a sinner.
Over whom, we are told, there is more joy in heaven than over the just man who needs no penance.
The more glory to Him, because there seemed no hope on earth that she could be saved.
Let us sing a song of thanksgiving﻿—let us glorify the only begotten Son of God, Who of His love and mercy will not let them perish whom He redeemed with His holy blood.
To Him be honour, glory, and praise through infinite ages. Amen.

The conversion of Thais by the hermit Paphnutius. Obedient to a vision, he leaves the desert, and, disguised as a lover, seeks out Thais in Alexandria. She is moved to repent by his exhortations and, renouncing her evil life, consents to be enclosed in a narrow cell, where she does penance for three years. Paphnutius learns from a vision granted to Anthony’s disciple Paul that her humility has won her a place among the blessed in Paradise. He brings her out of her cell and stays by her side until her soul has left her body.
Why do you look so gloomy, father Paphnutius? Why do you not smile at us as usual?
When the heart is sad the face clouds over. It is only natural.
I grieve over an injury to my Creator.
The injury His own creatures made in His very image inflict on Him.
Oh, father, your words fill us with fear! How can such things be?

It is true that the impassible Majesty cannot be hurt by injuries. Nevertheless, speaking in metaphor, and as if God were weak with our weakness, what greater injury can we conceive than this﻿—that while the greater world is obedient, and subject to His rule, the lesser world resists His guidance?
What do you mean by the lesser world?
It is not plain to many.

You know that the greater world is composed of four elements which are contraries, yet by the will of the Creator these contraries are adjusted in harmonious arrangement. Now, man is composed of even more contrary parts.
What can be more contrary than the elements?
The body and the soul. The soul is not mortal like the body, nor the body spiritual as is the soul.
That is true. But what did you mean, father, when you spoke of “harmonious arrangement”?
I meant that as low and high sounds harmoniously united produce a certain music, so discordant elements rightly adjusted make one world.
It seems strange that discords can become concords.
Consider. No thing is composed of “likes”﻿—neither can it be made up of elements which have no proportion among themselves, or which are entirely different in substance and nature.
One of the branches of the “quadrivium” of philosophy, my son. Arithmetic, geometry, music, and philosophy form the quadrivium.
I should like to know why they are given that name.
Because just as paths branch out from the quadrivium, the place where four roads meet, so do these subjects lead like roads from one principle of philosophy.
We had best not question you about the other three, for our slow wits can scarcely follow what you have told us about the first.
Still you might give us a general idea of the nature of music.
It is hard to explain to hermits to whom it is an unknown science.
Is there more than one kind of music?
There are three kinds, my son. The first is celestial, the second human, the third is produced by instruments.
In what does the celestial consist?
In the seven planets and the celestial globe.
Exactly as in instruments. You find the same number of intervals of the same length, and the same concords as in strings.
We do not understand what intervals are.
The dimensions which are reckoned between planets or between notes.
A tone is composed of two sounds, and bears the ratio of nine to eight.
As soon as we get over one difficulty, you place a greater one in our path!
That is inevitable in a discussion of this kind.
Yet tell us something about concord, so that at least we may know the meaning of the word.
Concord, harmony, or symphonia may be defined as a fitting disposition of modulation. It is composed sometimes of three, sometimes of four, sometimes of five sounds.
As you have given us these three distinctions, we should like to learn the name of each.

The first is called a fourth, as consisting of four sounds, and it has the proportion of four to three. The second is called a fifth. It consists of five sounds and bears the ratio of one and a half. The third is known as the diapason; it is double and is perfected in eight sounds.
And do the spheres and planets produce sounds, since they are compared to notes?
Why is the music not heard?
Yes, why is it not heard?

Many reasons are given. Some think it is not heard because it is so continuous that men have grown accustomed to it. Others say it is because of the density of the air. Some assert that so enormous a sound could not pass into the mortal ear. Others that the music of the spheres is so pleasant and sweet that if it were heard all men would come together, and, forgetting themselves and all their pursuits, would follow the sounds from east to west.
It is well that it is not heard.
We have heard enough of this kind of music. What of “human” music?
What do you want to know about that?

Not only, as I have already told you, in the combination of body and soul, and in the utterance of the voice, now high, now low, but even in the pulsation of the veins, and in the proportion of our members. Take the finger-joints. In them, if we measure, we find the same proportions as we have already found in concord; for music is said to be a fitting disposition not only of sounds, but of things with no resemblance to sounds.
Had we known the difficulty that such a hard point presents to the ignorant, we would not have asked you about your “lesser world.” It is better to know nothing than to be bewildered.
I do not agree. By trying to understand you have learned many things that you did not know before.
True it may be, but I am weary of this disputation. We are all weary, because we cannot follow the reasoning of such a philosopher!
Why do you laugh at me, children? I am no philosopher, but an ignorant man.
Where did you get all this learning with which you have puzzled our heads?
It is but a little drop from the full deep wells of learning﻿—wells at which I, a chance passerby, have lapped, but never sat down to drain.
We are grateful for your patience with us; but I for one cannot forget the warning of the Apostle: “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise.”
Whether a fool or a wise man does wrong, he will be confounded.
Nor is God offended by Knowledge of the Knowable, only by undue pride on the part of the Knower.

And I would ask you﻿—unto whose praise can the knowledge of the arts be more worthily or more justly turned than to the praise of Him Who made things capable of being known, and gave us the capacity to know them?
The more a man realizes the wonderful way in which God has set all things in number and measure and weight, the more ardent his love.
That is as it should be.
But I am wrong to dwell on matters which give you so little pleasure.
Tell us the cause of your sadness. Relieve us of the burden of our curiosity.
Perhaps you will not find the tale to your liking.
A man is often sadder for having his curiosity satisfied, yet he cannot overcome this tendency to be curious. It is part of our weakness.
Brothers﻿—there is a woman, a shameless woman, living in our neighbourhood.
A perilous thing for the people.
Her beauty is wonderful: her impurity is﻿—horrible.
Everyone has heard of her and her wickedness.
It is no wonder, for she is not satisfied to ruin herself with a small band of lovers. She seeks to allure all men through her marvellous beauty, and drag them down with her.
And it is not only fools and wastrels who squander their substance with her. Citizens of high standing and virtue lay precious things at her feet, and enrich her to their own undoing.
It is terrible to hear of such things.
Flocks of lovers crowd to her doors.
They are so crazed with desire that they quarrel and fight for admission to her house.
One vice brings another in its train.
They come to blows. Heads are broken, faces bruised, noses smashed; at times they drive each other out with weapons, and the threshold of the vile place is dyed with blood!
This is the injury to the Creator for which I weep day and night. This is the cause of my sorrow.
We understand now. You have good reason to be distressed, and I doubt not that the citizens of the heavenly country share your grief.
Oh, to rescue her from that wicked life! Why should I not try?
Brother, our Lord Jesus went among sinners.
She would not receive a hermit.
What if I were to go in the disguise of a lover?
If that thought is from God, God will give you strength to accomplish it.
I will set out immediately. I shall need your best prayers. Pray that I may not be overcome by the wiles of the serpent. Pray that I may be able to show this soul the beauty of divine love.
May He Who laid low the Prince of Darkness give you the victory over the enemy of the human race.
